title: Exposure: a service account key is on a public repository

lines.text: 11:05 report: key k-7f21 for sa-inventory-sync published on GitHub at 10:25; restock planning at 12:00

objective: Securing, auditing, and mitigating service account key usage
secondaryObjectives: Securing and protecting service accounts, including default ones

sources.cite: Google Cloud documentation, IAM: Delete and undelete service accounts
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: deleting a service account immediately cuts off applications that use it; a new account with the same name is a separate identity that does not inherit the old one's roles; undelete works for 30 days; 'If you're unsure whether anything still uses an account, Google recommends disabling it instead of deleting it.' Disabling a single key (gcloud iam service-accounts keys disable) and the audit log fields are from memory of the key management pages (to verify).

brief.situation: You are the security engineer at Fennick Outdoor. A researcher reports that a JSON key for sa-inventory-sync@fennick-prod was committed to a public GitHub repository 40 minutes ago. The same service account also runs the production inventory sync on GKE through an attached identity (no key) and feeds stock levels to the stores; the 12:00 restock planning reads them.
handover: The account has three user-managed keys: k-7f21 (the leaked one, made by a contractor), k-1a03 (unused since May), k-9b44 (used by a legacy on-premises job).
The organization policy to block new key creation is not yet enforced in fennick-prod.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the service account, its keys and attached identity, and who uses each.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: Restock planning reads stock levels at 12:00, 55 minutes after the report; meanwhile anyone holding the key can act as the account.

writeup.question: For the record: what was exposed and used, what you disabled and why not more, and what reduces the risk now.

parts.label: Exposed
parts.modelAnswer: Key k-7f21 of sa-inventory-sync was public from 10:25; audit logs show 185.220.101.7 listing the bucket and reading three stock exports at 10:51-10:52.

parts.label: Disabled
parts.modelAnswer: Disabled, then deleted k-7f21. The GKE sync uses an attached identity and the legacy job another key; deleting the account would have stopped both, and recreating it would not restore its roles.

parts.label: Risk now
parts.modelAnswer: The unused key is deleted, key creation is blocked by org policy, and the legacy job is planned onto Workload Identity Federation. The incident is recorded.

expertPath.text: Leaked key enabled; used from 185.220.101.7 to read 3 exports; GKE uses no key; legacy job uses k-9b44.
Disable and delete k-7f21; delete k-1a03; enforce key-creation policy; record.

saDeleted.headline: Kill the key, not the identity
saDeleted.body: A leaked key is one credential. Disable it (and delete it); the account and its other legitimate credentials stay. Deleting an account in use is an outage.

stillValid.headline: Minutes matter with a public key
stillValid.body: Disable a leaked key the moment you confirm it; then investigate what it did.

contained.headline: Good: precise containment
contained.body: You confirmed which key and what it had done, mapped who used which credential, disabled and deleted only the leaked key, verified it fails, and reduced standing keys for the future.

gaps.headline: Held, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria show what was left: the evidence before the change, the lasting step, the check, or the cause in the record.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: One user-managed key is public and has been used from outside to read objects. Disable that key now and then delete it: the account, its attached identity on GKE and the legacy job's key keep working. Deleting the whole account is an outage, and a recreated account does not get its roles back; the contractor's password is irrelevant. Then delete the unused key, block new keys and move the legacy job off keys.
